summary: Psalm 72 asks God to give the king justice and righteousness, then imagines a reign where the poor are defended, peace flourishes, and nations bring tribute. The poem expands from local judgment to worldwide dominion, then closes with praise to Yahweh and a notice that David's prayers have ended.
whyItMatters: This psalm closes Book II of Psalms with a royal prayer that measures kingship by justice for the needy and by blessing for the whole earth. Later Jewish and Christian readers have often heard messianic hope in it, but the chapter itself first presents an ideal prayer for the king.

context.author: The heading says, "By Solomon." In Psalms, such headings are ancient parts of the collection, but their exact force can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging, and readers debate the details.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving the psalm as prayer and hope.
context.date: Psalm 72 cannot be securely assigned to a single date. It belongs to a Psalter whose poems and collections developed over centuries, from the monarchy through the postexilic period.
context.setting: Book II of Psalms, which ends with this royal prayer and the notice, "This ends the prayers by David, the son of Jesse."
context.literaryForm: Hebrew royal psalm and prayer, using compressed poetry, parallel lines, images of creation and abundance, and a closing doxology.

outline.heading: Prayer for a just king
outline.note: The psalm asks God to give the king justice and righteousness so that he judges the poor rightly and breaks the oppressor.

outline.heading: Enduring peace and reverence
outline.note: The hoped-for reign is pictured as lasting across generations, refreshing like rain, and producing flourishing righteousness and peace.

outline.heading: Worldwide dominion and tribute
outline.note: The king's rule stretches from sea to sea, and distant rulers and nations are pictured bowing, bringing tribute, and serving him.

outline.heading: Why this reign deserves honor
outline.note: The explanation returns to the vulnerable: the king delivers the needy, has pity on the poor, and treats their blood as precious.

outline.heading: Blessing, abundance, and enduring name
outline.note: The poem asks for ongoing prayer and blessing for the king, abundant grain in the land, and a name through which all nations are blessed.

outline.heading: Praise and collection notice
outline.note: The psalm turns from the king to Yahweh God, blesses his glorious name, and closes Book II with a note about David's prayers.

keyVerses.text: By Solomon. God, give the king your justice; your righteousness to the royal son.
keyVerses.why: This opening names the psalm's request: the king's rule must depend on God's justice and righteousness.

keyVerses.text: He will judge the poor of the people. He will save the children of the needy, and will break the oppressor in pieces.
keyVerses.why: The verse shows what royal justice looks like in this psalm: protection for the poor and resistance to oppression.

keyVerses.text: He shall have dominion also from sea to sea, from the River to the ends of the earth.
keyVerses.why: This line marks the poem's large horizon, moving from the king's judgment within the people to dominion reaching the ends of the earth.

keyVerses.text: Praise be to Yahweh God, the God of Israel, who alone does marvelous deeds.
keyVerses.why: The closing praise keeps the final glory from resting on the king; Yahweh God alone is praised as the doer of marvelous deeds.

questions.question: Who is the king in this psalm?
questions.answer: The chapter opens, "By Solomon," and asks God to give justice to "the king" and righteousness to "the royal son." Readers differ on how to read the heading: it may point to Solomon, association with Solomon, or a Solomonic royal setting. The psalm itself focuses less on biography and more on the ideal shape of righteous kingship.

questions.question: What does the psalm mean by justice and righteousness?
questions.answer: In this chapter, those words are shown through action rather than defined abstractly. The king judges the people rightly, pays special attention to the poor, saves the children of the needy, and breaks the oppressor. The terms describe public rule that protects vulnerable people.

questions.question: Why are the poor and needy so central here?
questions.answer: The psalm repeats the poor and needy because they reveal whether the king's rule is just. Verses 12-14 say he delivers the needy when he cries, has pity on the poor and needy, and redeems their soul from oppression and violence. The chapter does not treat their suffering as incidental to kingship; it makes their protection a central test of it.

questions.question: Is the psalm claiming that one ancient king ruled the whole earth?
questions.answer: The poem uses expansive royal language: dominion from sea to sea, distant kings bringing tribute, and all nations serving the king. It begins as a prayer for justice and unfolds a vision of worldwide righteous rule. These are aspirations expressed in royal poetry, not a dated report that one historical king has already governed the whole earth.

questions.question: Why do mountains, rain, grain, and grass appear in a psalm about a king?
questions.answer: The psalm connects righteous rule with the flourishing of the land. Mountains and hills bring prosperity and righteousness, the king's coming is compared to rain on mown grass, and grain fills the land. These images make the reign feel life-giving, not merely powerful.

questions.question: What are Tarshish, Sheba, and Seba doing in the poem?
questions.answer: They represent distant regions whose kings bring tribute and gifts. Tarshish and the islands point toward the far west, while Sheba and Seba evoke lands to the south. Together they give geographic breadth to the next verse’s picture of all kings bowing and all nations serving.

questions.question: Does this psalm speak about the Messiah?
questions.answer: Later Jewish and Christian readers have often read Psalm 72 as messianic because its king is righteous, worldwide, enduring, and a source of blessing for all nations. The chapter itself first speaks as a royal prayer for the king and the royal son. A careful reading can name later messianic reception without skipping the psalm's immediate royal language.

questions.question: Why does the psalm end by praising Yahweh instead of the king?
questions.answer: After a long vision of royal greatness, verses 18-19 turn directly to Yahweh God, the God of Israel. They say he alone does marvelous deeds and ask that the whole earth be filled with his glory. The ending places the king's hoped-for reign under God's greater praise.

questions.question: What does the final sentence mean?
questions.answer: Verse 20 says, "This ends the prayers by David, the son of Jesse." In the shape of Psalms, this functions as a collection notice at the end of Book II. It does not mean there are no David-associated psalms later in the Psalter; it marks the close of this gathered section.

glossary.def: Right judgment and public fairness in the psalm, especially shown by defending the poor and needy.
The quality of rule requested from God for the king and associated with judging the people rightly.
The figure who harms the vulnerable and whom the king is expected to break in pieces.
Gifts brought by other kings as a sign of honor and submission to the king's dominion.
A closing word of affirmation in the doxology, repeated here as "Amen and amen."
